readingPassage.title: A1 reading: new student in Manchester
readingPassage.body: My name is Maya Patel. I am twenty years old and I am a new student at a language college in Manchester. Every weekday I wake up at seven, eat breakfast with my flatmates, and take the bus to campus. I study English in the morning and communication skills in the afternoon. After class I often go to the library because it is quiet and I can finish my homework there. On Saturdays I meet friends in a café near the station. We talk about our hometowns, hobbies, and future plans. My hometown is Leeds, but I like Manchester because it is bigger and more international. My hobby is photography. At the weekend I take photos in parks and museums. I want to introduce myself clearly, talk about study and work, and travel when my English improves. Teachers also ask students to write a short profile with nationality, occupation, and one hobby so classmates can practise greetings in pairs.

writing.title: Writing Task 1 — GT letter
writing.instruction: British Council GT Writing mock style: Task 1 letter. Spend about 20 minutes. Write at least 80 words. Cover every bullet. Classroom content — not a live IELTS prompt.
writing.prompt:
You want to join a class in Manchester about personal details. Write a letter to the school. In your letter:
• say who you are and what you do
• explain why you need the class
• ask two questions (times or fees)
Write at least 80 words.
writing.modelAnswer: Dear Sir or Madam, My name is Omar Hassan and I am a nurse in Manchester. I would like to join a class about personal details because I need clearer English for work and daily life. Could you tell me whether the Beginner English group still meets on Monday, and if the fee is forty pounds? I can start after seven o'clock. I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, Omar Hassan

writing.title: Writing Task 2 — Essay
writing.instruction: British Council Writing mock style: Task 2 essay. Spend about 25 minutes. Write at least 120 words. Give a clear position. Task 2 is worth more than Task 1.
writing.prompt: Some people think schools should spend more time on personal details. Others believe families should deal with this at home. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 120 words.
writing.modelAnswer: People disagree about who should lead on personal details. Schools can offer timed practice and feedback, which many adults in Manchester never get at home. Families, however, know personal routines and can support daily habits. In my view both sides matter: a short classroom task plus discussion at home is more effective than either approach alone. If the goal is an IELTS Writing score, learners also need word count, a clear position, and linking words — skills a school can teach more systematically than a busy household.

writing.title: Task 1 — Academic chart / table
writing.instruction: Academic Writing Task 1 style: summarise the information. Spend about 20 minutes. Write at least 80 words. Do not give opinions.
writing.prompt:
The table shows study hours in Manchester related to personal details.
Monday: 2 hours. Monday: 4 hours. Weekend: 1 hour.
Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 80 words.
writing.modelAnswer: The table compares weekly study time in Manchester. The highest figure is on Monday at four hours, while the weekend is only one hour. Monday sits in the middle at two hours. Overall, learners spend more time on a weekday session than at the weekend, so the main feature is an uneven weekly pattern rather than a flat routine.

writing.title: Coherence and cohesive devices

writing.modelAnswer: Weak control of daily routines causes missed details in listening and thin essays. Schools can set timed micro-tasks; learners can keep a phrase bank. Together these steps reduce panic on test day.

writing.title: Task 1 — Comparison
writing.instruction: Academic Writing Task 1 style: summarise the information. Spend about 20 minutes. Write at least 80 words. Do not give opinions.
writing.prompt:
The table shows study hours in Leeds related to daily routines.
Monday: 2 hours. Tuesday: 4 hours. Weekend: 1 hour.

writing.modelAnswer: The table compares weekly study time in Leeds. The highest figure is on Tuesday at four hours, while the weekend is only one hour. Monday sits in the middle at two hours. Overall, learners spend more time on a weekday session than at the weekend, so the main feature is an uneven weekly pattern rather than a flat routine.

writing.title: Task 2 — Advantage–disadvantage
writing.instruction: British Council Writing mock style: Task 2 essay. Spend about 25 minutes. Write at least 120 words. Give a clear position. Task 2 is worth more than Task 1.
writing.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of studying daily routines only online? Write at least 120 words.
writing.modelAnswer: Online study is flexible for a office worker in Leeds, but it can reduce speaking time. A mixed plan — online notes plus a weekly class — balances both.

writing.title: Task 2 — Opinion essay
writing.instruction: British Council Writing mock style: Task 2 essay. Spend about 25 minutes. Write at least 120 words. Give a clear position. Task 2 is worth more than Task 1.
writing.prompt: To what extent do you agree that daily practice is more important than long weekend study for daily routines? Write at least 120 words.
writing.modelAnswer: I strongly agree. Short daily sessions build fluency, while a rare long weekend often leads to forgetting. Timed official-style tasks during the week prepare candidates better.

writing.title: Coherence and cohesive devices
writing.instruction: British Council Writing mock style: Task 2 essay. Spend about 25 minutes. Write at least 120 words. Give a clear position. Task 2 is worth more than Task 1.
writing.prompt: Write an essay on daily routines using linking words (however, therefore, for example). Write at least 120 words.
writing.modelAnswer: People disagree about who should lead on daily routines. Schools can offer timed practice and feedback, which many adults in Leeds never get at home. Families, however, know personal routines and can support daily habits. In my view both sides matter: a short classroom task plus discussion at home is more effective than either approach alone. If the goal is an IELTS Writing score, learners also need word count, a clear position, and linking words — skills a school can teach more systematically than a busy household.

readingPassage.body: Last summer, Amina visited her grandparents in the countryside. The journey took four hours by bus, but she still remembers every detail. They walked in the hills every morning and cooked traditional meals together in the afternoon. One memorable evening they told family stories from decades ago. Amina also helped in the garden and learned the names of local plants. She says the trip was more than a holiday; it was an experience that changed how she thinks about free time. When friends ask what she achieved that year, she does not talk about certificates. She talks about patience, kindness, and the quiet joy of shared work. She hopes to return next year and keep a diary with photos, maps, and short notes in the simple past. readingPassage.title: A2 reading: Sofia's hometown
readingPassage.body: Sofia's hometown sits between green hills and a slow river. It is smaller than the capital and less crowded, but the streets feel spacious and friendly. Old stone houses resemble postcards, and the market square fills with music on Sundays. Visitors often comment on the appearance of flower balconies and the calm surroundings. Sofia's favourite place is a library with tall windows facing the park. She says the landscape looks different in each season: bright in spring, golden in autumn. Compared with big cities, public transport is slower, yet people smile more often. For Sofia, it is not the most famous place in the country, but it is the most peaceful place she knows, and she can describe it with clear comparatives. readingPassage.title: B1 reading: learning to swim
readingPassage.body: In my opinion, learning a practical skill is just as important as collecting certificates. Last year I taught myself to swim because I wanted to feel safer near water. At first I assumed it would be easy, but progress was slow. I considered quitting after two weeks, yet I continued because each small improvement gave me confidence. The main advantage was independence: I could join friends at the pool without fear. The drawback was time; evening practice made my schedule tighter. From this perspective, useful skills grow from patience and clear reasons. When people ask why I value swimming, I say it supports health and calm thinking. I now advise classmates to choose one skill, practise regularly, and measure progress with real situations, not only grades. Opinion language with because/since/as makes arguments easier to follow in interviews and essays. In speaking Part 2, a useful structure is: state the skill, explain how you learned it, give one advantage, admit one drawback, and finish with your opinion today. readingPassage.title: B1 reading: plans and conditions
readingPassage.body: Next year I intend to take the IELTS exam again if my band score is below my goal. I am likely to study listening every morning and writing every weekend. My main goal is a balanced score across all four skills. If I achieve the target, I will apply for a graduate course abroad. If I do not reach it, the consequence will be another two months of focused practice rather than giving up. I also plan to join a speaking club because conversation improves fluency under pressure. Teachers say a clear outcome helps students stay motivated. I agree. When friends ask about my future, I do not only list dreams; I describe steps, dates, and what I will do if the first plan fails. Real progress needs both ambition and a realistic backup plan written with first conditional forms. First conditional sentences sound natural when both parts are realistic: a present condition and a future result you can actually control or prepare for. Next year I intend to take the exam again if my score is below target. I am likely to practise listening every morning and writing each weekend. If I achieve the goal, I will apply for a course abroad. If not, the consequence will be two more months of focused study rather than quitting.

readingPassage.title: B2 reading: social media debate
readingPassage.body: Social media has become a controversial part of modern life. On the one hand, it connects families across countries and helps students find learning materials quickly. Furthermore, small businesses can reach customers without expensive advertising. Nevertheless, significant problems remain. Misinformation spreads fast, and many users struggle with distraction or addiction. Critics argue that the drawbacks outweigh the benefits for teenagers who sleep less and compare themselves constantly. Supporters reply that education and clear rules can mitigate harm without banning the tools completely. In balanced essays, writers should present both sides, use cohesive devices carefully, and finish with a measured judgement. Technology is not simply good or bad; its impact depends on design, habits, and responsibility. Heading-matching practice rewards readers who track each paragraph's function. Cohesive devices only help when each paragraph has one job. If you add furthermore without a new supporting idea, the essay becomes repetitive instead of balanced. Social media connects families and helps learners find materials quickly. Furthermore, small businesses can advertise cheaply. Nevertheless, misinformation and distraction are significant problems. Critics argue drawbacks outweigh benefits for teenagers. Supporters reply that education can mitigate harm. A balanced conclusion avoids absolute claims. Readers preparing for matching-headings tasks should label each paragraph with a short function note before they look at the option list.  Furthermore, controversial claims need evidence; nevertheless, essays that only list connectors without ideas score poorly.  Significant progress comes from timing: skim for structure first, then scan for detail. Mitigate panic by practising with two paragraphs a day until the method feels automatic.

readingPassage.title: B2 reading: urban data lecture
readingPassage.body: Today's lecture focused on how urban data is collected and analysed by city planners. Several surveys were conducted across five cities, and the results were compared using shared indicators such as traffic delay and park access. Sensors were installed on major roads, and anonymised mobile data was used to estimate evening movement patterns. Researchers argued that better evidence should be implemented in transport policy before expensive projects begin. A key hypothesis was that small design changes can reduce crowding more cheaply than building new highways. Subsequent discussion examined privacy limits and the cost of maintaining open data systems. Overall, the session showed that modern planning comprises both technical measurement and public trust. Academic listening and reading often hide key facts inside passive verb phrases. Academic listening rewards notes that capture passive processes, numbers, and contrasts. Write short cues such as 'surveys conducted' or 'hypothesis tested' rather than full sentences. Several surveys were conducted across five cities, and results were compared using shared indicators. Researchers argued better evidence should be implemented before expensive projects begin. Formal register also appears in emails and reports where actions are described without naming every actor.  Hypotheses are stated carefully, subsequent results are compared, and recommendations are implemented only after checks.  A useful revision habit is to highlight every passive verb, then ask whether an active alternative would be clearer for a personal reflection task.

readingPassage.title: C1 reading: growth, environment, and nuance
readingPassage.body: Whether governments should prioritise economic growth over environmental protection remains a multifaceted debate. Short-term growth can create jobs and fund public services, yet it may also underpin patterns of consumption that damage ecosystems. A nuanced policy recognises the discrepancy between quarterly targets and long-term resilience. Evidence from energy transitions can substantiate claims that green investment supports innovation rather than blocking prosperity. Still, the paradigm of endless expansion faces criticism from economists who warn about inequality and resource limits. Effective argumentation avoids absolute claims and uses hedging language where uncertainty exists. In advanced discussion, speakers evaluate trade-offs, test assumptions, and ask who benefits from each choice. The strongest answers are not the loudest; they are the ones that connect principles to practical consequences with clear structure and credible support. Advanced answers show control under pressure: define terms, acknowledge counter-arguments, hedge uncertain claims, and close with a judgement that follows from the evidence you actually used. Multifaceted topics punish speakers who chase slogans instead of mechanisms. Practise transforming a simple opinion into a nuanced position by adding conditions, stakeholders, and time scales. When you substantiate a point, name the source type—study, example, or principle—so the examiner can track your reasoning. Discrepancies between ideals and budgets are often the most honest place to begin a C1 discussion. Whether governments should prioritise economic growth over environmental protection remains multifaceted. Short-term growth can fund services, yet it may underpin unsustainable consumption. Evidence can substantiate claims that green investment supports innovation. Multifaceted policy debates punish binary thinking. Speakers who can underpin a claim, substantiate it, and still admit uncertainty sound more credible than speakers who chase volume.  Practise reframing a simple slogan into a nuanced position by naming stakeholders, time horizons, and trade-offs.  When a discrepancy appears between ideals and budgets, treat it as the start of analysis rather than a reason to abandon the topic.  C1 performance is less about rare vocabulary and more about controlling complex sentences under time pressure while remaining precise.

audioLines: City Language Centre, hello. I'd like a class about abstract argumentation.
Name? Nadia El-Sayed. Nationality? Egyptian.
The Advanced seminar group is on Wednesday in Room 4.12. The fee is ninety pounds.
Welcome to the Cambridge centre. Sports are in Room 4.12. The café opens at five o'clock. Do not park by the main door.
Your project is about abstract argumentation. I interviewed a policy analyst. Only ten minutes were recorded. Let's meet on Wednesday.
Today's lecture looks at abstract argumentation. In Cambridge the monthly cost was ninety pounds. Daily habits mattered more than rare long sessions.

questions.question: Part 2. Visitors may park by the main door.
Part 3. The whole interview was recorded.

speaking.title: Part 1 — introduction and interview (4–5 min)
speaking.instruction: British Council Academic mock: several short familiar questions. Answer in full sentences.
speaking.examinerQuestion: Let's talk about you. Do you work or study, and what do you like doing in Cambridge?
speaking.modelAnswer: I'm a policy analyst in Cambridge. In my free time my hobby is debate.
speaking.tip: Part 1 should be natural and not a memorised speech.

speaking.title: Part 2 — long turn with 1 min notes (3–4 min)
speaking.instruction: Cue card: 1 minute notes, then up to 2 minutes speaking.
speaking.examinerQuestion: Describe a time you practised abstract argumentation.
speaking.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a Wednesday in Cambridge. I practised abstract argumentation with Helena near Room 4.12. At first I was slow, but a simple example helped me keep going for two minutes.
speaking.tip: Use the bullets. Keep speaking until the examiner stops you.

speaking.title: Part 3 — two-way discussion on Part 2 theme (4–5 min)
speaking.instruction: More abstract follow-up. Give a position, a reason, and an example.
speaking.examinerQuestion: How can cities like Cambridge help people improve skills related to abstract argumentation?
speaking.modelAnswer: Public classes, libraries, and timed practice help more than studying alone. For example, a short evening course in Room 4.12 gives feedback you cannot get from an app.
speaking.tip: This part is discussion, not yes/no.

reading.title: Reading paper (passage stays visible)
reading.instruction: Inspera-style: keep the text on screen. True/False/Not Given and completion.
reading.passage: A community project in Cambridge helps adults practise English through abstract argumentation. Classes meet on Wednesday in Room 4.12. The advertised fee is ninety pounds. Nadia El-Sayed, a policy analyst, says short daily tasks beat rare long weekends. The organisers have not published exam scores for every student, so success is described with attendance and teacher comments. Parking is limited; the notice does not mention childcare. Quiet study after five o'clock is encouraged.

questions.question: Every student receives a published exam score.
questions.explanation: Scores have not been published for every student.

questions.question: The project provides childcare.
questions.explanation: Childcare is not mentioned as provided; the notice does not mention it.

writing.title: Writing Task 2 — essay
writing.instruction: British Council mock: Task 2. About 40 minutes. At least 250 words. Task 2 is worth more than Task 1.
writing.prompt: Some people think daily practice is the best way to improve abstract argumentation. Others prefer one long session at the weekend. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
writing.modelAnswer: Daily practice builds habit and reduces panic, which matters in Cambridge for a busy policy analyst. A long weekend session can feel productive but is easy to skip. I believe a short official-style task most days, plus one longer review, is the most realistic plan.

examFramework.awardingBody: British Council, IDP IELTS, Cambridge University Press & Assessment
examFramework.notes: IELTS is not a pass/fail CEFR exam. Candidates receive a band 0–9 for Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking; overall is the average rounded to the nearest 0.5. Practise the official computer/online samples first: Listening (once only, questions on screen), Academic Reading in the Inspera player, British Council GT Writing (Task 1 letter 150 words + Task 2 essay 250 words), and British Council Academic Speaking (Parts 1–3 with a Part 2 cue card). In-app papers are original classroom tasks in those shapes, not live test content. Academic and General Training share Listening and Speaking; Reading texts and Writing Task 1 differ.
examFramework.passRule: No pass mark. Overall band = mean of four skills, rounded to nearest 0.5.

listening.example: A conversation about travel arrangements, then a talk about local facilities, a seminar discussion, and a lecture. Heard once; 40 questions in recording order.

Part 3 — two-way discussion on Part 2 theme (4–5 min)

parts: General Training: Section 1 short notices, Section 2 workplace texts, Section 3 longer general-interest text

parts: Task 1 Academic: describe a graph/table/chart/diagram (≥150 words, ~20 min)
Task 2: discursive essay (≥250 words, ~40 min; counts more)
